If people already ask you to cook for birthdays, naming ceremonies or church events, you have the most important ingredient: food people enjoy. Catering adds three things on top of good cooking. **Scale**: you cook five or ten times more than usual, in bigger pots, with more gas and more hands. **Responsibility**: the people eating are not your family, and some may be elderly, pregnant, very young or allergic. **Time pressure**: the food must be ready, hot and safe at an exact time, in a place that is not your kitchen.

Choosing your first job size

Your capacity is set by your biggest pot, your number of burners, your fridge or freezer space, your helpers and your transport. A good rule is to start with a job you could almost do twice over, so a delay or a burnt pot does not ruin the event. Many new caterers start with 20 to 50 guests and grow from there.
Worked example: is a 40-pack office lunch realistic?

For example, Amaka in Ibadan is asked to deliver 40 packs of jollof rice, chicken and coleslaw to an office by 1:00 pm on a weekday. She has a two-burner gas cooker, one large pot, a medium pot and one helper.
She lists the work: about 5 kg of raw rice, 40 chicken pieces, one batch of coleslaw, 40 packs to fill and label.
Her large pot cooks about 3 kg of rice at once, so the rice needs two batches of roughly 75 minutes each, about 2.5 hours.
Chicken boiling and frying on the second burner takes about 2 hours, running at the same time as the rice.
Coleslaw and packing with her helper takes about 1 hour, plus 45 minutes to drive to the office.
Working back from 1:00 pm with a 30-minute buffer, she needs to start cooking by about 7:00 am.
The job fits her equipment if she starts at 7:00 am and preps vegetables the evening before. A 150-pack order the same day would not fit, so she would decline it or hire extra pots and help.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that almost 1 in 9 people in the world fall ill every year after eating contaminated food. Most of that illness is preventable. WHO teaches food handlers everywhere a simple set of rules called the **Five Keys to Safer Food**. They are easy to remember and they work in a home kitchen, a canteen or a hired kitchen behind an event hall.
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly

Check all five keys for every dish on your menu, not only the meat.
A person washing hands at a sink
Key 1 starts with hands: wash before cooking and after anything dirty.
Key 1: Keep clean

Germs that cause food poisoning live on hands, cloths, chopping boards and surfaces. Wash your hands with soap and clean running water before handling food, often during cooking, and always after using the toilet, touching raw meat, fish or eggs, handling money, blowing your nose or taking out the rubbish. Rub every part of the hands, including between fingers and under nails, then rinse and dry with a clean towel. If you have no tap, set up a bucket with a tap or ask a helper to pour water.
Tie hair back or cover it, remove rings and bracelets, and keep nails short.
Wear a clean apron, and keep it for cooking only.
Wash and sanitise boards, knives and worktops after raw meat or fish.
Keep insects, rats, cats and dogs away from food and the cooking area.
Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut on the hand should not handle food that day.
Key 2: Separate raw and cooked

**Cross-contamination** means germs moving from raw food to ready-to-eat food. It happens when the same board is used for raw chicken and then for coleslaw cabbage, when raw meat drips onto salad in a fridge, or when the bowl used to marinate chicken is reused for cooked chicken. Use separate boards and knives for raw meat and fish, or wash them well in between. Store raw meat in covered containers below cooked food in the fridge or freezer.
Key 3: Cook thoroughly

Cook meat, poultry, eggs and seafood until the centre reaches **70°C**, the temperature on WHO's Five Keys poster. Chicken juices should run clear, not pink, but a probe thermometer is far more reliable than looking. Bring soups and stews to the boil. When you reheat cooked food, heat it until it is steaming hot all through.
Key 4: Keep food at safe temperatures

Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Keep hot food piping hot, above 60°C, until serving, and keep cold food cold, below 5°C. The next lesson covers this key in detail because it is where most catering problems happen.
Key 5: Use safe water and raw materials

Use safe, treated water for cooking, washing salad and making ice. Buy fresh meat and fish from sellers who keep them cool and clean. Reject swollen, rusted or dented cans, mouldy grains and spices, and food past its expiry date. Wash fruit and vegetables well, especially anything eaten raw like cabbage, carrots, cucumber and lettuce.
Worked example: applying the Five Keys to one menu
For example, Funmi is catering a 60-guest naming ceremony with jollof rice, fried chicken, coleslaw and moi moi.
Keep clean: she sets up a handwashing point with soap and a towel at the kitchen door and asks both helpers to wash on arrival and after every raw-meat task.
Separate: she uses a red board for raw chicken and a green board only for cabbage and carrots, and keeps the coleslaw covered on a separate table.
Cook thoroughly: she checks the thickest chicken pieces with a probe thermometer and confirms 70°C or more before frying.
Safe temperatures: coleslaw stays in a cooler with ice packs, the rice and chicken go hot into insulated coolers.
Safe water and raw materials: she washes the cabbage in treated water and buys eggs for the moi moi from a trusted seller, checking for cracks.
Every dish, not just the chicken, has a clear safety control, and each helper knows their role.

Train your helpers on the Five Keys before every job, not only the first time. A two-minute briefing at the start of the day works well: where the handwashing point is, which board is for raw meat, which table is for ready-to-eat food, and who checks temperatures. Helpers copy what they see, so let them see you wash your hands and change boards every time.
Salads and raw vegetables are high risk
Coleslaw and salad are not cooked, so nothing kills germs that land on them. Wash vegetables in safe water, use clean boards, keep them cold, and dress them as close to serving as you can.

Bacteria that cause food poisoning grow fastest at warm temperatures, roughly the heat of a Nigerian afternoon. WHO's Five Keys poster marks the range between **5°C and 60°C** as the **danger zone**. Below 5°C growth slows right down. Above 60°C most of these bacteria cannot grow. Between the two, numbers can double quickly. Catering is mostly about keeping food out of this zone, or moving it through quickly.

Different countries draw the danger zone slightly differently. For example, the United States Department of Agriculture uses about 4°C to 60°C, and the UK uses 8°C to 63°C for its legal limits. In this course we use WHO's 5°C and 60°C, which is simple and safe.
Why rice needs special care

Cooked rice is one of the riskiest foods at Nigerian parties because so much of it is cooked early and kept warm for hours. Uncooked rice can carry spores of a bacterium called *Bacillus cereus*. Cooking does not kill all the spores. If cooked rice sits warm for hours, the spores grow and make toxins that reheating does not destroy. The answer is simple: keep cooked rice hot above 60°C, or cool it quickly and refrigerate it, never leave it sitting warm on the counter.
Cooling food quickly
Spread hot food into shallow trays or several small containers, not one deep pot.
Stand containers in a basin of cold water with ice, stirring stews now and then.
Once steam stops rising, cover and refrigerate, aiming to be below 5°C well within the 2-hour room-temperature limit.
Label each container with the dish and the date it was cooked.
Use refrigerated cooked food within a short time, and when in doubt, throw it out.
Using a probe thermometer

A digital probe thermometer costs far less than one lost client. Push the tip into the thickest part of the meat, away from bone, or into the centre of a pot of rice or stew after stirring. Wait until the number stops changing. Clean the probe with hot soapy water or a sanitiser wipe between foods, especially between raw and cooked. Check it now and then in boiling water: it should read close to 100°C.
Worked example: a holding plan for a 1:00 pm serving
For example, Chioma finishes cooking jollof rice and chicken at 10:30 am for a birthday party that serves food at 1:00 pm. She has two insulated coolers and a probe thermometer.
10:30 am: she checks the rice at 85°C and the chicken at 78°C, then fills the coolers hot and closes them immediately.
She warms each cooler first with hot water for 10 minutes and empties it, so the cold walls do not chill the food.
12:15 pm at the venue: she opens one cooler briefly and the rice reads 68°C, still above 60°C.
1:00 pm: serving starts, and she keeps lids closed between servings.
3:30 pm: leftover rice reads 52°C, below 60°C, and has been out of safe holding for an unknown time, so she does not take it home for resale.
Her food stayed above 60°C for the whole 2.5-hour hold. She records the readings as evidence of safe practice.
Smell and taste are not safety tests
Food carrying harmful bacteria or toxins can look, smell and taste normal. Do not decide safety by tasting. Decide by time and temperature.

Ice also matters. Ice made from unsafe water can carry germs into drinks and salads, so make ice from treated or boiled and cooled water, or buy it from a seller you trust. Keep ice for drinks separate from ice used to chill coolers and bottles, and never use your hands to scoop it: use a clean scoop or cup.
Write temperatures on a simple log sheet: dish, time, reading, initials. It takes seconds, it trains your helpers, and it gives you evidence if a client ever asks how you keep food safe.

A good event menu is not just a list of dishes you cook well. It is a set of dishes that suit the guests, survive the journey, stay safe for hours, fit your equipment and fit the client's budget. Before you suggest anything, ask the right questions.
Questions to ask before you plan
Date, venue and the exact serving time. Is there a kitchen or power at the venue?
Number of adult guests and children, and whether guests come and go or sit at once.
Format: food packs, buffet, served table or small chops.
Budget per head or total budget.
Must-have dishes, for example jollof rice, fried rice, ofada with ayamase, pounded yam and egusi, or asun.
Allergies, religious needs such as no pork, and vegetarian guests.
Who serves: your staff, the client's ushers, or guests themselves.
A plate of rice with stew
Rice dishes travel and hold well, which is why they anchor most Nigerian party menus.
Build the plate first

Think of one guest's plate. A balanced Nigerian party plate usually has a **starch** (jollof or fried rice, ofada, swallow), a **protein** (chicken, beef, turkey, fish), a **side** (moi moi, plantain, coleslaw or salad) and sometimes a **small extra** (a bottle of water, a small chops pack). Planning by plate helps you count portions and price per head later.
Pick dishes that hold well

Some foods stay good in a hot cooler for three hours. Others go soggy, dry or unsafe. Fried plantain softens, salad wilts once dressed, and pounded yam forms a skin and hardens. Jollof rice, fried rice, stews, moi moi and well-cooked meats hold better. Plan the hard-to-hold items for last-minute work, or swap them out.

Worked example: from budget to menu

She checks capacity: two big pots of rice, one pot for moi moi in leaves or tins, chicken boiled and fried on the third burner.
She asks about allergies and learns one guest cannot eat groundnut, so no groundnut-based pepper mix goes on the chicken.
She sends the client two options: Option A as above, and Option B with fried rice and turkey at a higher price.
The client gets a clear, costed choice, and every dish on it can be cooked, held and delivered safely with Halima's equipment.

Step 2 and 3: Multiply and add a buffer

Multiply each portion by the number of guests. Then add a buffer, usually around 10 percent, because guest numbers grow, servers give bigger spoons and some food is lost when packing. Children may eat less, so if the client says 100 guests including 30 children, you may plan the children at a smaller pack size. Agree the final number in writing.
Worked example: jollof rice and chicken for 50 and 100 guests
For example, Ngozi uses her tested portions: 120 g raw rice and one chicken piece per adult. She cuts each bird into 8 pieces. She plans a 10% buffer.
Rice for 50 guests: 50 × 120 g = 6,000 g = 6 kg. Add 10%: 6 × 1.1 = 6.6 kg. She buys 7 kg.
Rice for 100 guests: 100 × 120 g = 12 kg. Add 10%: 12 × 1.1 = 13.2 kg. She buys 14 kg.
Chicken for 50 guests: 50 pieces × 1.1 = 55 pieces. 55 ÷ 8 = 6.9, so she buys 7 birds.
Chicken for 100 guests: 100 × 1.1 = 110 pieces. 110 ÷ 8 = 13.75, so she buys 14 birds.
Coleslaw for 100 guests: 100 × 80 g = 8 kg, plus 10% = 8.8 kg of finished coleslaw.
For 100 guests she shops for 14 kg of rice, 14 birds and enough cabbage, carrots and dressing to make about 9 kg of coleslaw, with a small buffer and no wild over-buying.
Scaling a recipe

Your home recipe may serve 10. To scale it, find the **scaling factor**: new number of servings ÷ original number of servings. For 100 guests from a recipe for 10, the factor is 100 ÷ 10 = 10. Multiply every ingredient by 10. For 50 guests, the factor is 5.
Worked example: scaling a jollof base from 10 to 50 servings
For example, Ngozi's family jollof for 10 uses 1.2 kg rice, 1 kg tomato and pepper blend, 300 g onions, 250 ml vegetable oil and 1.2 litres of stock.
Scaling factor: 50 ÷ 10 = 5.
Rice: 1.2 kg × 5 = 6 kg. Blend: 1 kg × 5 = 5 kg. Onions: 300 g × 5 = 1.5 kg.
Oil: 250 ml × 5 = 1.25 litres. Stock: 1.2 litres × 5 = 6 litres.
Salt, stock cubes and pepper: she starts with about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then tastes and adjusts.
Her biggest pot holds about 3 kg of rice, so she cooks two batches of 3 kg, each with half the scaled ingredients.
She has a clear scaled recipe and knows it must be cooked in two batches, which she adds to her cooking timetable.
Not everything scales in a straight line

Seasoning, liquid and cooking time do not always multiply perfectly. Big pots lose less water to steam, and strong spices add up fast. Season gradually and taste. Never cram a pot beyond its size: rice cooks unevenly and the bottom burns.
Step 5: Round to market units

Markets sell in bags, crates, baskets and local measures that vary from place to place. Turn your totals into what you will actually buy: kilograms of rice, a crate of eggs (30 eggs), a number of whole birds, litres of oil. If you buy by a local measure, weigh one measure at home once so your list matches reality. Keep the list in the same order as the market route to save time.

Production day is where planning meets the pot. A clear timetable, a tidy kitchen layout and a packed equipment box let you stay calm, keep food safe and arrive on time. Most catering disasters come from no buffer time, not from bad cooking.
Work backwards from serving time

Start from the moment guests eat and walk backwards: set-up time at the venue, travel time, loading, packing, and each cooking task. Add a buffer for traffic, a late gas refill or a power cut. The aim is to finish cooking close enough to serving that food can be held hot safely, but not so late that you rush.

Worked example: a 100-pack timetable
For example, Ronke caters 100 packs of jollof rice, chicken, moi moi and coleslaw for a 1:00 pm church anniversary, 45 minutes away. She has a three-burner cooker, two helpers and preheated coolers.
Day before: shop, steam moi moi and cool it fast in shallow trays, make stew base and refrigerate, wash and shred cabbage and carrots, chill.
6:30 am: boil chicken on burner 1, start rice batch 1 on burner 2, heat stew base to boiling on burner 3.
8:30 am: rice batch 2; fry chicken in turns; reheat moi moi by steaming until hot through.
10:00 am: probe-check chicken at 70°C or above and rice above 60°C; mix coleslaw dressing and keep it cold.
10:15 to 10:45 am: pack food into preheated coolers, coleslaw into an ice-packed cooler; 11:00 am leave; 11:45 am arrive and set up.
Food is cooked by 10:00 am, held hot for 3 hours or less, and Ronke has 75 minutes of buffer between arrival and serving.
A delivery van on the road
Transport is part of food safety: food must travel hot, cold and covered.
Zones that stop cross-contamination
**Raw zone**: one table and board for raw chicken, meat and fish, with its own knife and a bin.
**Cooking zone**: burners and pots, with clean spoons that never touch raw meat.
**Ready-to-eat zone**: coleslaw, packing and serving, wiped and sanitised, away from raw work.
Wash hands every time you move from the raw zone to any other zone.
Use colour-coded or clearly marked boards and bowls, and keep cooked food covered.
Holding and transport

Preheat insulated coolers with hot water for 10 minutes, empty them and fill with very hot food. Fill them well, because a half-empty cooler loses heat faster. Keep cold foods in a separate cooler with ice packs. Load coolers flat, wedge them so they cannot slide, and never put raw items in the same box as ready food. At the venue, keep lids closed until serving and check temperatures.

The last hour is where good work is often undone. Guests crowd the table, helpers are tired and dishes are left open in the heat. Set up a serving station before guests arrive: a clean table, chafing dishes lit and hot, serving spoons and tongs for each dish, and a covered spare cooler under the table. Your own hours of shopping, cooking, packing and delivering are a real cost. If you leave them out, your 'profit' is really your wage, and you cannot grow or hire help later. Always tell the client what portion they are paying for so there are no surprises.

A food allergy is when the body's immune system reacts to a normal food as if it were dangerous. Reactions can be mild, like an itchy mouth, or severe and life-threatening, with swelling of the throat and difficulty breathing. Cooking does not remove most allergens. For an allergic guest, even a small trace from a shared spoon can be enough.

The UK Food Standards Agency lists 14 allergens that food businesses there must declare: celery, cereals containing gluten (such as wheat), crustaceans (such as crayfish, prawns and crab), eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs (such as snails and periwinkle), mustard, tree nuts, peanuts (groundnuts), sesame, soya, and sulphur dioxide or sulphites. Nigeria's rules may differ, but this list is a useful, recognised checklist for any caterer.

On the day: prevent cross-contact

**Cross-contact** is when a small amount of an allergen gets into a food that should not contain it. Cook the allergen-free portion first, in clean pots with clean spoons, before the kitchen is full of crayfish and groundnut dust. Pack it separately, seal it and label it clearly with the guest's name or the words 'No groundnut' or 'No crayfish'. Give it directly to the client or host, not to a general usher.
Worked example: one guest with a groundnut allergy
For example, Halima is catering 80 packs and the client says the bride's sister has a severe groundnut allergy. The menu includes suya-spiced chicken.
She checks every dish: the suya spice contains groundnut, and her chin chin is fried in the same oil as groundnut snacks.
She cooks one pack first: plain peppered chicken, jollof rice and coleslaw, with clean pots, spoons and fresh oil.
She seals it in a separate container, labels it 'NO GROUNDNUT: for Aisha', and stores it in its own bag.
At the venue, she hands it to the client personally and explains what is in it.
She leaves chin chin out of that pack because she cannot guarantee no cross-contact.
The allergic guest gets a safe meal, the client sees real care, and Halima is honest about what she cannot guarantee.
If you do not know, say so

If a guest asks whether a dish contains an allergen and you are not sure, say 'I am not sure, so please do not eat it.' Never guess. If someone has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or collapses after eating, call for emergency help and get them to a hospital immediately.

Cover cuts on hands with a waterproof plaster and wear a glove over it.
Respect religious diets honestly: never serve pork or non-halal meat as halal.

Ask for feedback the right way

The Five Keys to Safer Food

Key one. Keep clean. Wash hands with soap and clean running water before handling food, and after the toilet, raw meat, money or rubbish. Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut should not handle food that day.
Key two. Separate raw and cooked. Use separate boards and knives for raw meat, and store raw meat covered, below cooked food in the fridge.
Key three. Cook thoroughly. Meat, poultry and eggs must reach 70 degrees Celsius at the centre.
Key four. Keep food at safe temperatures. We will look at this closely in a moment.
Key five. Use safe, treated water and good raw materials. Reject swollen or dented cans, mouldy grains and food past its expiry date.

Ask every client about allergies, and write the answer on the job sheet, not only in a chat. Halima's client said the bride's sister has a severe groundnut allergy.
Halima checked every dish. The suya spice contains groundnut, and her chin chin is fried in the same oil as groundnut snacks.
She cooked one pack first, before the kitchen was full of groundnut dust, with clean pots, spoons and fresh oil.
She sealed it and labelled it, no groundnut, with the guest's name, and left out the chin chin she could not guarantee.

She handed it to the client personally. If a guest asks and you are not sure, say: I am not sure, so please do not eat it. If someone has trouble breathing or swelling after eating, call for emergency help and get them to a hospital immediately.

Ronke's quote of 420,000 naira asks for a 50% deposit, 210,000, before she buys any ingredient. The balance is due two days before the event. She confirms every payment in her banking app and sends a receipt with the amount, date and balance remaining.
Fraudsters send fake SMS and screenshot alerts. Never trust them. Write your guest-count and cancellation terms on the quote, so they are agreed before any money moves.

Hazard, control, check
Funmi's safety plan for coleslaw
Buy: firm vegetables, sealed salad cream
Prepare: safe water, green board, clean hands
Store: covered, in the fridge below 5°C
Mix: dress on the morning, keep chilled
Transport: own cooler with ice; log 4°C
Each step: what could go wrong, what stops it, how will I check?
Professional kitchens use a system called HACCP. Its thinking is simple. For each step, ask what could go wrong, what stops it, and how you will check.
Funmi plans 9 kilograms of coleslaw for 100 guests. Coleslaw is never cooked, so every step matters. She buys firm, fresh vegetables and salad cream with an intact seal and a valid date.
She washes the vegetables in safe water, uses the green ready-to-eat board, and washes her hands first.
The shredded vegetables go into covered containers in the fridge, below 5 degrees, overnight.
She adds the dressing on the morning of the event, in a sanitised bowl, and keeps it chilled.

It travels in a separate cooler with ice packs. She records 4 degrees at packing, and checks again on arrival. Write clear steps a helper can follow: check chicken at 70 degrees is clearer than cook properly.
